newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian interest rates to rise in 1997/98-NatWest.
newsitem.headline: Indian interest rates to rise in 1997/98-NatWest.

text.p: Indian interest rates will rise in 1997/98 (April-March) "although the current situation of excess liquidity will depress them in the first half of FY98," NatWest Securities said in a research report.
The Reserve Bank of India is widely expected to announce measures in its April 15 monetary policy to prompt interest rate cuts, bankers and analysts said.
One of the measures is expected to be a reduction in the ceiling of 10 percent interest on deposits up to one year.
NatWest said credit demand was still poor and the industrial turnaround that the 1997/98 budget intends to stimulate will take time to show results.

"We expect the turnaround will begin by June-July 1997. Meanwhile, the deposit growth continues to be high. The downward pressure on nominal rates will therefore persist and the PLR (prime lending rate) will fall," it said.
It said a fuel price hike was in the offing.
Inflation in manufactured commodities will rise in the second half of 1997/98 with the surge in consumption demand.
"In sum, the average inflation is likely to go up in 1997/98 to around 8.2 percent," NatWest said.
It said the cumulative effect of the erosion in the PLR and high inflation will be to pull real interest rates down sharply in the first half of 1997/98, it said.
The second half will see effect of budget provisions exerting upward pressure on interest rates, it predicted.
"The corporate tax and customs duty concessions granted by the budget will revive business confidence - we forecast that manufacturing will post an 11 percent plus growth in FY98."
Lower rates of personal tax effected by the budget will improve consumption demand and demand for credit, NatWest said.
India's state-run banks are also set to borrow more in 1997/98 to make up for less budgetary support, it said.
"The incremental credit deposit ratio of banks will thus move from the current level of 0.3 to 0.6 by end-FY98 and put pressure on the PLR," it predicted.
The government's borrowing is also expected to push up interest rates, NatWest said.

"Though the budget provides only for an increase of 15 billion rupees in the government's market borrowings, we feel that the budget's revenue targets might be overoptimistic by about 50 billon rupees," it said.
To that extent, the government will have to borrow more, it said.
As real interest rates continue to fall in the first half of 1997/98, there will be a deceleration in deposit growth.
"By the second half of FY98, the current excess liquidity will slowly turn tight, and start nudging the PLR up."
As PLR is likely to rise more than inflation, the real interest rates will rise in the second half. "However, average real interest rates in FY98 will be lower than in FY97."
